Ludwig's Advice
It's June 2033. Jakob comes down to Ludwig's on the ground floor one evening. He has a little velvet box in his pocket. He wants to ask Mara to marry him, but he doesn't know how.
Ludwig, can I ask you something? It's… personal.
If it's about the little box in your jacket pocket that you've been clutching for ten minutes: yes.
Is it that obvious? Oh no. Yes. It's a ring. The ring my grandmother wore for fifty years. I want to ask Mara if she'll marry me. But I don't know how.
And how did you imagine it?
If I were braver, I'd have asked her last year already. In a restaurant, with candles, with champagne. But that's not us. Mara doesn't like grand gestures.
That's not quite true. She doesn't like grand gestures that mean nothing. What does she think of when she thinks of you?
The choir, I think. Where we met. And my cello. She always says that when I play, she hears what I can't say.
There you go. On the twenty-first it's the Festival of Music. Jonas's choir is singing in Kollwitzpark. And a cellist who met a woman in that very choir could play a song that's just for her.
In front of three hundred people? I'd be shaking like a leaf.

Of course you'd be shaking. I was shaking too, in 1972, with my guitar, at the Fairy-Tale Fountain. And do you know what? Ingrid said she didn't fall in love with me because of the song. But because I played anyway.
And her parents? Shouldn't I ask her father first?
You should have done that long ago. Call Dan. Andrei will translate. And then, my boy, you practise every evening. I can hear it through the ceiling, believe me.

Maras Vater Dan
Das Lied aus Thüringen

The surprise had been prepared for three weeks, and it was a miracle that Mara hadn't noticed anything. Perhaps it was because, as the new head nurse, she was working so much that in the evenings she just collapsed into bed, exhausted. Perhaps it was because the whole house was playing along, with a discipline that reminded Ludwig of his days at the transport company. Every evening when Mara had a late shift, Jakob practised in Ludwig's flat on the ground floor, because from there you couldn't hear it on the fourth floor. And every evening Ludwig sat in Ingrid's armchair and listened, with his eyes closed, and at the end he said the same thing every time: “Once more. More slowly. So that she hears every note.”

The others helped, each in their own way. Lena invented a reason why Mara absolutely could not be on duty on the twenty-first and persuaded the stand-in on ward 4 to swap with Mara. Andrei organised the plane tickets for Dan and Elena in secret, and Kuba and Ola picked them both up from the airport, with a sign that said in big letters “FAMILIA IONESCU”. Grete insisted on correcting Jakob every Wednesday after Elif's piano lesson: “Too fast. Too loud. A marriage proposal is not a march, young man. It's a lullaby.”

The song wasn't a famous piece. It was an old folk song from the village in Thuringia where Jakob had grown up, a song about a well and a linden tree, which his grandmother Hilde had sung to him when he was little, every evening before he fell asleep. She had given him the cello when he was seven, an old, second-hand child's cello, which she had bought with the money from her chickens. And when she died nine years ago, she had left him two things: her ring, slim and golden, with a small blue stone, and a note on which was written in her shaky handwriting: “For the right one. Play her our song.”

A week earlier, Jakob had called Sibiu. Andrei sat next to him and translated, and Jakob had three pages of notes in front of him, with all the sentences he wanted to say, in perfect, polite German, with lots of Konjunktiv. He didn't need them. After the first sentence, Dan, the quiet beekeeper, interrupted him and said something in Romanian that Andrei at first didn't want to translate, because he had to laugh. Then he translated it anyway: “Dad says: at last. He's been waiting for this for two years. He asks why it took you so long. And he says you mustn't make her cry, unless it's for joy.”

On the twenty-first of June, a warm Tuesday evening, Kollwitzpark was full of people. Everywhere in Prenzlauer Berg there was music, on every corner, in every courtyard, on every balcony: jazz and rock and folk music and an old man with an accordion who stood in front of the bakery. On the little stage in the park Jonas's choir was singing, forty voices, and in the second row stood Mara, who had been singing with them every Thursday for four years. She didn't know that in the front row of the audience sat two people who had flown in from Sibiu that morning: a tall, quiet man with hands that smelled of honey, and a small woman in a navy-blue dress, who was so nervous that she was holding her husband's hand so tightly it hurt.

After the third song, Jonas came to the microphone. “Dear people,” he said, “we have a guest today. A cellist who came to this choir a few years ago because he didn't know anyone in Berlin. Here he met someone. And he wants to tell her something he can't say. That's why he's playing it.” Mara looked around, puzzled. And then Jakob came up onto the stage, with his cello, in a white shirt that Lena had ironed that afternoon, and sat down on a chair, right in front of the second row. In front of Mara.
Ludwig, who was sitting in the front row next to Dan, laid his hand for a moment on the tall, quiet man's arm. Dan didn't understand a word of German, but he understood the gesture and nodded.

He was trembling. You could see it in his hands when he raised the bow. But he played anyway. He played the song from Thuringia, the song about the well and the linden tree, slowly, the way Ludwig had taught him, so that she would hear every note. The park went quiet. People who had just been laughing and drinking stopped talking. Even the old man with the accordion in front of the bakery stopped playing. And Mara stood in the second row of the choir, between a soprano from Kreuzberg and a bass from Pankow, and very slowly understood what was happening here.

She didn't recognise the song. She had never heard it. But she recognised the way Jakob played: like on that evening three years ago, when he had unpacked his cello for the first time in Ludwig's flat, and like every Sunday morning since then, when he thought she was still asleep and practised quietly in the living room. He played the way he spoke when he wanted to say something important: slowly, carefully, with little pauses, as if he first had to check every word. And suddenly Mara understood why she hadn't had a single late shift in the last three weeks, why Lena had laughed so strangely, why her mother had sounded so flustered on the phone.

When the last note had faded, Jakob laid the cello carefully on the floor. He stood up. He knelt down in front of Mara, on the dusty wood of the little stage, in front of forty singers and three hundred spectators, and took the little velvet box out of his pocket. His hands were shaking so badly that he could hardly open it. Then he said, and his voice was quiet, but in the silence of the park everyone heard it: “Mara. My grandmother said I should play our song to the right one. I've never played it for anyone. Until today. Will you marry me?”

Mara said nothing. She stood there, with the sheet music in her hand, and cried. Then she looked over Jakob's shoulder into the audience and saw, in the front row, her father and her mother. Dan gave her a nod, slowly, with the serious face he also had with his bees. Elena had put both hands to her mouth. And next to them sat Ludwig, with the old brass doorbell in his hand, ready. Mara looked at Jakob again, who was still kneeling and still trembling, and said, in German and then once more in Romanian, so that her parents would understand too: “Ja. Da. Yes, of course, you silly thing. Da.”

And then Ludwig rang the bell. Once, loud and clear, across the whole of Kollwitzpark. And three hundred people applauded, and the choir spontaneously began to sing, and the old man with the accordion played a wedding march, out of tune, loud and wonderful. Jakob put the ring on Mara's finger, Hilde's ring, slim and golden, with the small blue stone, and it fitted perfectly, as if it had been made for her. Dan stood up, went to the stage, took Jakob's face in his big hands that smelled of honey and said the only German word he had secretly learned in three weeks: “Willkommen.” (Welcome.)

Elena hugged her daughter for so long that Jonas had the choir sing another song, just to gain time. Then she hugged Jakob, then Ludwig, whom she hadn't seen since their visit to Berlin five years ago, when he had taken Dan up to the roof with the bees, and said to him in her new, careful German, which she had been practising since Lena's visit at Christmas: “Thank you, Mr Brandt. For everything. You took care of my daughter.” Ludwig shook his head. “No, Mrs Ionescu,” he said. “Your daughter took care of us. Of the whole house. From the very first day.”

Later, much later, when the music in the courtyards was dying down and the lamps in the park were coming on, they were all sitting in the café “Bei Ingrid”: Mara and Jakob, Dan and Elena, Lena and Andrei, Ludwig, Grete and Friedrich, Susanne and Peter, Thomas, Anja and Leo, the Yilmaz family, Kuba and Ola, Michael from Munich, Jonas and Clara with little Ludwig, who was four by now and had fallen asleep on Ludwig's lap. Andrei wrote something in the brown notebook, which after almost five years was finally full, on the last page. He didn't read it to anyone. But Lena read it later, secretly, while he was asleep.

“Kastanienallee 31, June 2033. Six years ago, a nurse from Sibiu came to this house with a suitcase and a dictionary. She hardly knew any German. She didn't know anyone. Today she said yes in Kollwitzpark, in German and in Romanian, in front of three hundred people who are all her neighbours. This notebook is full. Tomorrow I'll buy a new one. It will need lots of stories.”
